Persona 1 of 4
System Administrator
The operational backbone — manages pipeline health, user accounts, FERPA compliance, generation limits, and data integrity. The admin rarely interacts with content; they keep the system trustworthy.
Admin · I / Navigation Architecture

Eight sections — operations, compliance, and system health

The admin persona is unlike any other in Journey OS. Where faculty create and students consume, admins maintain trust. Their navigation is organized around system health (Dashboard, Pipeline), user management (Faculty, Students), compliance (FERPA, Data Integrity), and operational controls (Generation Limits, Settings). Every admin action is consequential — modifying user permissions, reviewing FERPA logs, retrying failed pipelines — and the UI reflects that seriousness.

Admin · II / Dashboard + Action Queue

The severity-sorted action queue — highest impact first, every time

The admin dashboard is not a metrics display — it's a triage center. The action queue surfaces everything that requires human intervention, sorted by impact severity. A critical pipeline failure that is blocking faculty from generating questions appears above a routine pending enrollment. The admin should be able to open Journey OS, see the queue, work through it top-to-bottom, and be done. Nothing important should be buried.

Admin · III / Pipeline Health

Real-time visibility into P1, P2, and P3 — with dead letter queue management

Dead letter queue — the safety net

Every Inngest function has an onFailure handler that writes to pipeline_dead_letters after all retries are exhausted. This table carries: event name, payload, error message, stack trace, retry count, and faculty ID. The admin can inspect any dead letter, retry it manually with an override (e.g., reduced batch size), or mark it as permanently failed. Faculty are notified when their pipeline items enter the dead letter queue so they know something went wrong.

Generation limits (C10)

Three-layer rate control: (1) per-faculty concurrent limit (max 3 simultaneous P3 runs per faculty_id via Inngest concurrency key), (2) per-faculty daily limit (tracked in generation_daily_usage — default 100 items/day, configurable per faculty), (3) institution-level monthly budget cap (tracked in institution_generation_limits — default $500/month, triggers alert at 80%). Admin can view current usage, adjust limits per faculty, and see cost breakdown by course and faculty member.

Admin · IV / User Management

Faculty + students — approval, accommodations, and account health

Faculty management

Pending faculty appear with their registration details (MSM email, department, role claim). Admin approves or rejects. Approved faculty get role = 'faculty' on their Supabase auth.users row and a corresponding Faculty node in Neo4j. Admin can suspend (immediately revokes access), reset generation limits, view usage history, or transfer courses if a faculty member leaves.

Faculty flags visible to admin: awaiting_approval, generation_limit_exceeded, items_pending_review_aging (items sitting in review for >30 days — FERPA alert), suspended, inactive_30d.

Student management + ADA accommodations

Students can be enrolled manually (by admin) or via SIS integration. ADA accommodations are stored in student_accommodations table: accommodation_type (extended_time, separate_room, reader, etc.), multiplier (1.5x, 2.0x time), and effective_date. When an exam is administered, the exam delivery engine checks this table and adjusts the timer for the specific student. The accommodation record is FERPA-protected — only admins and the individual student's advisor can view it.

FERPA — the non-negotiable

Student educational records are protected by FERPA. In Journey OS, this means: (1) The FERPA audit log is written by a Postgres trigger at the database level — it cannot be bypassed by application code. (2) The log is immutable — rows can be inserted but never updated or deleted, even by service_role. (3) Only the admin and the student's assigned advisor can access student performance data. Faculty see aggregate course data but never individual student answers to questions. (4) The FERPA audit log search is read-only even for admins — no deletions, no exports without a logged reason.

Advisor · II / Dashboard + At-Risk Classification

Three gap types — isolated, cluster, or systemic — determine the intervention

The at-risk gap type classifier

Not all gaps are the same. An advisor looking at a student with poor Renal scores needs to know: is this a single isolated concept they haven't seen yet? Is it a cluster of related concepts (Renal physiology + acid-base + diuretics) that point to a foundational misunderstanding? Or is it a systemic pattern — low mastery across multiple unrelated organ systems — suggesting an engagement or study method problem rather than a content gap? The three classifier types determine the intervention recommendation: for isolated gaps, suggest targeted practice; for cluster gaps, suggest reviewing the foundational concept and its downstream effects; for systemic gaps, flag for an in-person advisor meeting and possibly learning support services.

Key finding

Bloom levels 5 and 6 (Evaluate and Create) are consistently undercovered across all systems — averaging 18% coverage institution-wide. This aligns with known USMLE Step 1 difficulty: the hardest questions require evaluation and synthesis. Faculty need targeted prompts to generate higher-Bloom items. The Chair can use the "Fill Bloom 5-6 gaps" action to trigger generation campaigns for the specific system × Bloom cells that are below 40%.

Chair · III / Standard Setting + Item Quality

Angoff simulation, KR-20 reliability, DIF analysis — defensible cut scores

Why standard setting matters

A passing score on a medical school exam should be defensible: it should represent a judgment by qualified faculty about what a minimally competent student should be able to do, not an arbitrary percentage. The Angoff method asks faculty to judge, for each item: "What percentage of minimally competent students would answer this correctly?" The average of these judgments becomes the cut score. Journey OS implements this as a simulation tool — showing faculty the item stem and options, collecting Angoff ratings, computing the aggregate cut score, and comparing it against the actual score distribution. This produces a legally and academically defensible pass/fail threshold.

Cut score of 62% is supported by Angoff data (4 raters, good agreement). Passing rate of 78% is within normal range for M2 pre-clerkship exam. KR-20 = 0.74 indicates good reliability. Recommended: adopt 62% as official cut score for this exam.
DIF analysis — differential item functioning by subgroup

DIF identifies items that perform differently for identically-able students from different demographic groups (gender, URM status). An item with high DIF may be biased. Items flagged for DIF are not automatically removed — they trigger a faculty review. The Chair reviews flagged items and decides whether to remove, revise, or retain with documentation.

Dean · II / LCME Readiness Room

58 LCME elements — evidence status, DCI export, and gap triage

The LCME Readiness Room

LCME accreditation requires medical schools to demonstrate compliance with 58 Elements organized into 12 standards. For the Dean, Journey OS becomes an evidence management system: for each element, it shows what data Journey OS can contribute to the DCI (Data Collection Instrument), what evidence status that data has (confirmed vs. partial vs. gap), and provides a one-click export formatted for DCI submission. This is the feature that makes Journey OS relevant at the most senior level of the institution.

DCI export package — what Journey OS provides
The export generates a structured evidence package for Elements 8.1–8.6 including: item bank statistics (count by course, Bloom distribution, QA score summary), exam administration records (dates, student counts, pass rates), psychometric summary (KR-20 per exam, DIF results, p-value distributions), USMLE coverage matrix (all 18 systems × 6 Bloom levels), and BKT mastery aggregate by cohort.
Dean · III / Equity Dashboard

DIF analysis, URM/gender performance gaps, Cohen's d over time

Why the equity dashboard matters institutionally

LCME Standard 3.3 requires medical schools to maintain institutional policies for fair and appropriate treatment of all medical students. The equity dashboard operationalizes this requirement: it surfaces performance gaps between demographic groups on the same assessment items, computed using Cohen's d (effect size). A gap of d > 0.5 (medium effect) triggers a review. The dashboard tracks gaps over time to determine whether they are growing, stable, or closing — helping the Dean understand whether institutional interventions are working.

Renal gap widening

The Renal system gap grew from d=0.41 to d=0.54 over 12 months. This is the only system showing consistent widening. Likely cause: Renal content is undertaught (41% coverage vs 86% for Cardiovascular) — URM students with fewer outside study resources are disproportionately affected by content gaps in the institutional item bank.

Institutional maturity model
Current stage: Level 3 of 5

Level 1: Item bank exists. Level 2: Systematic generation. Level 3: Psychometric QA (current). Level 4: Adaptive delivery + BKT at scale. Level 5: Continuous equity monitoring with automated interventions. The Dean can view evidence for each level and what actions advance the institution to the next stage.
